# Investigative Report: Linking the Ronin Bridge and Harmony Horizon Bridge Thefts to Lazarus Group

## Executive assessment

The available public evidence supports a strong link between the March 2022 Ronin Bridge theft and the June 2022 Harmony Horizon Bridge theft through three overlapping elements: **public attribution to North Korea’s Lazarus Group, similar laundering behaviors, and blockchain-wallet activity consistent with a coordinated North Korean hacking operation**.

The Ronin theft involved approximately **173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC**, valued at approximately **$540 million when the theft occurred**. The Harmony Horizon Bridge theft involved approximately **$99.7 million**, commonly described as a $100 million theft. Elliptic attributed the Ronin theft to Lazarus Group in March 2022, with the U.S. Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) subsequently identifying the relevant Ethereum address as belonging to Lazarus Group. In May 2023, the FBI publicly confirmed that Lazarus Group was responsible for the Harmony theft. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The laundering evidence is also materially consistent. In both cases, the stolen assets were moved through intermediary wallets, decentralized exchanges, cross-chain mechanisms, and privacy-enhancing services. The Ronin laundering pattern included conversion of USDC into ETH, use of Tornado Cash, swaps into Bitcoin, Bitcoin mixing, and eventual movement toward crypto-to-fiat services. The Harmony laundering pattern included programmatic structuring through Tornado Cash, later movement through Railgun, and deposits into centralized exchanges including Binance and Huobi. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

In my assessment, the evidence is sufficient to conclude that the two thefts are linked at the **public attribution and behavioral-pattern levels**. The provided materials do not, however, contain specific wallet addresses, transaction hashes, or a direct wallet-to-wallet bridge between the Ronin and Harmony cases. They therefore support a high-confidence **group-level linkage**, but not an independently reproducible address-level proof based solely on the supplied material. The supplied sources also do not establish that Lazarus Group is identical to **APT38**. That relationship should remain unconfirmed in this report.

## Scope and source assessment

This report uses only the four source URLs supplied in the case materials. The materials contain three substantive case reports and one Elliptic resource-index page.

| Source ID | Publisher and date | Primary evidentiary value |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | Elliptic, March 29, 2022 | Initial attribution and laundering analysis for the Ronin theft; later OFAC attribution |
| S2 | Chainalysis, September 8, 2022 | Laundering typology, cross-chain tracing, and seizure information for Ronin funds |
| S3 | Elliptic, May 9, 2023 | FBI confirmation of Lazarus attribution for Harmony; Tornado Cash and Railgun tracing |
| S4 | Elliptic resource page | General Elliptic research index; no additional substantive case evidence in the supplied content |

The strongest evidence is S3 for Harmony because it reports an FBI confirmation, and S1 for Ronin because it records the subsequent OFAC designation of the relevant Ethereum address. S2 provides useful corroboration from an independent blockchain-analytics company concerning Ronin’s laundering stages and the seizure of more than $30 million. S4 is not relied upon for any material factual conclusion because the supplied text is an index page rather than a case-specific report.

## Case 1: Ronin Bridge theft

### Attack and value

The Ronin Network theft was announced on March 29, 2022, after occurring six days earlier. The stolen assets consisted of **173,600 ETH and 25.5 million USDC**. Elliptic valued the theft at approximately **$540 million at the time of the theft**, while noting that the assets were worth more than **$615 million when the exploit was discovered**, reflecting cryptocurrency price changes. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

According to the cited postmortem summary, the attacker obtained the private keys of **five of Ronin’s nine validator nodes**, which was sufficient to authorize withdrawals. The attack was assessed by Ronin as socially engineered rather than the result of a technical flaw in the bridge’s smart-contract logic. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

### Attribution

Elliptic reported that OFAC identified the Ethereum address associated with the theft as belonging to **Lazarus Group**, described in the source as a North Korean state hacking group. The OFAC action prohibited U.S. persons and entities from transacting with that address. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

This is significant because the attribution was not limited to a private analytical assessment by Elliptic. The source reports a subsequent public sanctions action by a U.S. government authority identifying the address as Lazarus Group-linked. On the evidence provided, the Ronin attribution is therefore supported by both private-sector analysis and government action.

### Laundering pattern

The Ronin laundering sequence described by Chainalysis contains approximately five stages:

1. Stolen Ether was sent to intermediary wallets.
2. Ether was mixed in batches using Tornado Cash.
3. Ether was exchanged for Bitcoin.
4. Bitcoin was mixed in batches.
5. Bitcoin was deposited with crypto-to-fiat services for cash-out.

Chainalysis also reported that more than **12,000 cryptocurrency addresses** had been used in the laundering process at the time of publication. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

Elliptic described an initial phase in which the stolen USDC was exchanged for ETH through decentralized exchanges. This reduced exposure to asset issuers that might freeze stablecoins and avoided the screening associated with centralized exchanges. The attacker then moved approximately **$16.7 million in ETH through three centralized exchanges**, before shifting toward Tornado Cash after the exchanges publicly indicated that they would cooperate with law enforcement. Elliptic reported that approximately **$80.3 million in ETH** had been sent through Tornado Cash by April 14, 2022, with another **$9.7 million** held in intermediary wallets apparently prepared for laundering. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge))

The exact figures reported by Elliptic and Chainalysis are not necessarily intended to be identical. They were published on different dates, used different analytical methodologies, and may refer to different stages or categories of the movement. The common pattern, however, is clear: rapid movement through intermediary wallets, asset conversion, use of mixers, and attempts to reach cash-out points.

## Case 2: Harmony Horizon Bridge theft

### Attack and value

The Harmony Horizon Bridge was exploited on June 24, 2022, for approximately **$99.7 million**, generally rounded to $100 million. Elliptic described the bridge as servicing the Harmony blockchain and noted prior concerns that it was overly centralized and therefore vulnerable to social engineering. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The supplied evidence does not provide the individual wallet addresses involved in the Harmony theft. It does, however, describe the movement of the stolen funds through specific privacy-oriented services and exchanges.

### Attribution

Elliptic reported that the **FBI confirmed Lazarus Group’s responsibility** for the Harmony Horizon Bridge theft. The FBI confirmation also validated Elliptic’s earlier assessment, which had been based on similarities between the Harmony laundering activity and patterns observed in prior Lazarus-linked blockchain thefts. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

This is the strongest direct link between Harmony and the Lazarus-linked Ronin case: the Harmony report explicitly states that the attribution was based in part on similarities with the laundering methods used after the Ronin Bridge theft. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

### Laundering pattern

After the Harmony theft, the attackers programmatically structured transactions through **Tornado Cash**, an Ethereum-based decentralized mixer. Elliptic stated that the laundering methods mirrored those used to conceal funds from the Ronin Bridge theft. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Elliptic estimated that more than **$555 million** from the Ronin and Harmony thefts had been sent through Tornado Cash: more than **$468 million from Ronin** and approximately **$96 million from Harmony**. The source characterized this combined activity as approximately **5.8% of nearly $9 billion** in total funds sent through Tornado Cash at that time. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

After Tornado Cash sanctions, the Harmony funds were later moved through **Railgun**, a privacy-oriented decentralized-finance protocol. Elliptic estimated that approximately **70% of the Ether passing through Railgun** at the relevant time represented funds from the Harmony theft. The report argued that this unusually high concentration made the mixing less effective because the anonymity set was comparatively small. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

The funds were subsequently deposited into three crypto-asset exchanges. Elliptic reported that Binance and Huobi identified, blocked, and seized a portion of the funds. ([Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

## Comparative linkage analysis

| Linkage dimension | Ronin Bridge | Harmony Horizon Bridge | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public attribution | OFAC identified the relevant Ethereum address as Lazarus Group | FBI confirmed Lazarus Group responsibility | Strong group-level linkage |
| Attack context | Cross-chain bridge theft involving validator-key compromise | Cross-chain bridge theft; source describes centralization and social-engineering exposure | Similar target type and attack context, but not proof by itself |
| Initial laundering | Intermediary wallets, DEX conversion, ETH movement | Programmatic structuring through Tornado Cash | Consistent use of staged laundering |
| Privacy services | Tornado Cash; later cross-chain DeFi activity | Tornado Cash followed by Railgun | Strong behavioral overlap |
| Cross-chain behavior | Chain-hopping across Ethereum, BNB Chain, and BitTorrent Chain | Movement through Ethereum-based privacy infrastructure and exchanges | Consistent with multi-chain concealment |
| Exchange exposure | More than $30 million seized with industry and law-enforcement cooperation | Binance and Huobi blocked and seized part of the funds | Similar cash-out disruption pattern |
| Address-level evidence in supplied material | No readable addresses supplied | No readable addresses supplied | Direct wallet linkage cannot be independently reconstructed |

The clearest linkage is not simply that both were bridge attacks. It is that the same actor attribution is supported by government statements and that the laundering behavior displays repeated operational characteristics: intermediary wallets, automated or structured transfers, asset swaps, mixers, cross-chain movement, and attempts to reach centralized exchanges or cash-out points.

Chainalysis specifically described North Korea’s “typical DeFi laundering technique” as a sequence involving intermediary wallets, Tornado Cash, conversion to Bitcoin, Bitcoin mixing, and crypto-to-fiat services. It also reported that, after OFAC sanctions against Tornado Cash, the Ronin-linked actors used DeFi services to chain-hop across multiple assets and blockchains. ([Chainalysis, 2022](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/axie-infinity-ronin-bridge-dprk-hack-seizure/))

## Wallet evidence and limitations

The supplied evidence refers to wallet activity but does not reproduce wallet addresses or transaction hashes. The Ronin evidence identifies a thief’s Ethereum address through the OFAC attribution described by Elliptic, while the Harmony evidence describes clusters of intermediary addresses, post-Tornado withdrawals, Railgun deposits, and exchange deposits. ([Elliptic, 2022](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/540-million-stolen-from-the-ronin-defi-bridge); [Elliptic, 2023](https://www.elliptic.co/insights/fbi-confirms-north-korea-s-lazarus-group-as-hackers-behind-100-million-harmony-horizon-bridge-theft))

Accordingly, the wallet evidence supports the following limited conclusions:

- Wallet activity was central to attribution and laundering analysis.
- The Ronin activity included thousands of addresses and multiple laundering stages.
- The Harmony activity included intermediary wallets, Tornado Cash, Railgun, and exchange deposits.
- The two cases shared laundering infrastructure and transaction-structuring characteristics.
- The supplied materials do not permit an independent analyst to reproduce the complete transaction graph or identify a specific wallet that directly transferred funds from the Ronin cluster to the Harmony cluster.

This limitation matters. A behavioral similarity is probative, but it is not equivalent to a cryptographic or transaction-level proof. The public attribution evidence substantially strengthens the linkage, particularly because the FBI confirmation for Harmony and OFAC attribution for Ronin independently point to Lazarus Group. Nevertheless, the report should not claim a direct wallet bridge that is not shown in the provided materials.

## Lazarus Group and APT38

The task refers to “Lazarus Group/APT38.” The supplied sources identify Lazarus Group and describe it as North Korean-backed or state-linked, but they do **not** mention the designation “APT38.” No source provided here establishes that the Ronin and Harmony operations were conducted by an entity specifically labeled APT38, nor does any supplied source explain whether APT38 is a synonym, subordinate unit, or separate designation from Lazarus Group.

Therefore, the defensible conclusion is:

> The Ronin and Harmony thefts are publicly linked to Lazarus Group. The supplied evidence does not independently establish an APT38 attribution or a Lazarus Group–APT38 equivalence.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a strong and concrete conclusion that the Ronin Bridge and Harmony Horizon Bridge thefts are linked through Lazarus Group attribution and repeated laundering behavior. Ronin was publicly associated with Lazarus Group through OFAC attribution of the relevant Ethereum address, while the FBI later confirmed Lazarus Group responsibility for Harmony. The laundering patterns in both cases involved intermediary wallets, structured transaction flows, asset conversion, Tornado Cash, cross-chain or DeFi-based obfuscation, and attempted movement into centralized exchanges.

The relationship is strongest at the level of **actor attribution and operational methodology**. It is weaker at the level of directly demonstrable wallet-to-wallet continuity because the supplied materials do not include the relevant addresses or transaction identifiers. The sources support a high-confidence assessment that the same North Korea-linked hacking organization, publicly identified as Lazarus Group, conducted both thefts or controlled the laundering operations associated with both incidents. They do not support a separate, source-grounded conclusion that the actor should specifically be labeled APT38.
